title: Atomic output frames and restartable tool transactions PRD (draft)
body:
Summary:

This PRD proposes a combined approach to two related pain points we see with hosted streaming responses + tool calling: (1) clients struggling to safely consume partially emitted structured output (JSON/frames) without brittle parsers or reconstruct/replay work, and (2) tool integrations (database writes, externals, side-effects) that cannot be made idempotent or resumed reliably when streaming or network failures occur.

Proposal in one line: introduce an atomic-output framing protocol plus a restartable transaction abstraction for tool calls, surface easy SDK helpers for common client patterns, and provide server-side guarantees (at-least-once with detectable duplicates and transactional boundaries) so apps can resume mid-stream without data corruption or complex reconciliation.

Why this matters (problem description):
- Many customers build UIs that update incrementally from streaming responses. When structured output (e.g., arrays of records, tool-call blocks) is emitted piecemeal, clients either: (a) buffer and wait for final parse, hurting latency, or (b) incrementally parse partial JSON which is fragile and error-prone.
- Tool calls triggered mid-stream (e.g., write_order, charge_card, create-ticket) create irreversible side effects. If a client reconnects or the stream restarts, teams must implement complex dedup keys and reconciliation logic.
- SDK teams report developers frequently copy-pasting ad-hoc patterns (sequence numbers, checkpoints) and still seeing edge-case bugs in flaky networks and mobile clients.

Goals / success metrics (90-day and 6-month):
- Reduce customer-reported incidents related to partial-JSON parsing by 80% within 3 months for beta testers.
- Provide SDK-level primitives that reduce median developer integration time (first working implementation) from ~3 days to <1 day.
- Allow safe resumed streams with no duplicate side-effects in 95% of beta scenarios (measured via synthetic tests against retries/failures).
- Add tracing/telemetry so that prefix cachehit rate and replay rates are observable (target: replay <1% of streams after rollout).

User stories / scenarios:
- Web product: incremental list UI renders items as they arrive. If the socket drops and reopens, the UI should resume and continue adding new items without re-applying old ones or leaving partial broken JSON.
- Payments integration: model triggers a charge via tool_call. If the client reconnects mid-stream, the charge must not be applied twice; however, the client should be able to resume the stream and see a final confirmation frame.
- Mobile offline: client goes offline, then restarts stream later from last checkpoint; server provides frames since that checkpoint and tool-calls preserve idempotency or provide compensating metadata.

Design overview (high level):
1) Atomic Output Frames (AOF)
   - Server emits discrete, self-contained frames rather than arbitrary text chunks. Each frame has a small header (frame_id, seq, type, opaque_bucket_id) and a payload which is a JSON blob or binary blob. Frames can represent: record, array-chunk, tool-call-intent, tool-result, checkpoint, error, or end-of-stream.
   - Frames are syntactically complete and parseable independently. Clients can render frames as they arrive without needing to buffer for later completion.
   - For arrays/streams of records, the server emits element frames and periodic 'array-fence' frames indicating logical boundaries for safe commits.

2) Restartable Tool Transactions (RTT)
   - Tool-call frames include a transaction token and semantics: tentative, commit, abort. A typical sequence: tool-call-intent(frame) -> tool-executing(frame) -> tool-committed(frame) or tool-aborted(frame).
   - Each transaction token is client-visible and derived deterministically by server+request input (or client-provided idempotency key when available). The server records the transaction token in a durable index so duplicate intents can be detected and short-circuited into a tool-result frame referencing previous outcome.
   - By separating 'intent' and 'commit', external side effects can be performed under guard rails (e.g., a confirmed commit frame only follows a successful external operation). If a reconnection causes the same intent to be re-sent, server returns existing commit result instead of re-executing.

3) SDK ergonomics and helpers
   - High-level SDK methods: watchStream({onFrame, onCheckpoint, onToolEvent, resumeFrom}) that manage reconnect/backoff, automatic resume tokens, and idempotency.
   - Small, composable parsers for common UI patterns: incrementalListRenderer, chunkedArrayMerger, toolTransactionListener. These are shipped in JS, Python, and Go SDKs.
   - A lightweight browser-only helper that stores last-seen checkpoint in localStorage for immediate resume after temporary disconnects.

API surface and protocol details (examples):
- Frame envelope (conceptual):
  {"frame_id":"f_0001","seq":42,"type":"record","checkpoint":false,"payload":{...}}
- Tool intent example:
  {"frame_id":"f_0100","seq":101,"type":"tool_intent","tool":"charge-card","tx_token":"tx:23a1","payload":{"amount":1250,"currency":"usd"}}
- Tool committed example returned on success:
  {"frame_id":"f_0101","seq":102,"type":"tool_commit","tx_token":"tx:23a1","result":{"status":"ok","charge_id":"ch_8a9"}}
- Checkpoint frame to enable resume:
  {"frame_id":"f_0200","seq":150,"type":"checkpoint","checkpoint_token":"cp:20251103-01","description":"safe to resume from this token"}

Guarantees and failure semantics:
- Parse-safety: any frame is individually parseable. Partial delivery only affects whole frames; clients will not receive partial-frame JSON.
- Tool deduplication: intents deduplicated via tx_token and server log; replays return committed result. If external system provides no idempotency, server stores mapping for a configurable retention window (default 7 days) to avoid accidental duplicates.
- At-least-once vs exactly-once: we provide at-most-once effect for most managed tools by detection and lookup (effectively making them idempotent to clients), but we still classify some third-party connectors as at-least-once if they cannot be wrapped. UIs should show pending/confirmed states accordingly.

Observability and telemetry:
- Emit events per frame (frame_emitted, frame_ack, checkpoint_created, tool_intent_logged, tool_commit) with route/model/request tags.
- Add a dashboard showing resumed-stream rate, average reconnection latency, tx_token collision rate, and duplicate-tool-event rate.

Rollout plan and gating:
- Phase 1 (beta, internal + selected customers): SDK + server supports AOF and RTT for a subset of managed tools (tickets, user-profiles) and streaming read-only records. Collect integration feedback (4 weeks).
- Phase 2 (wider beta): extend to payments and 3rd-party connectors with additional audits and optional longer dedup retention. Add language SDKs and browser helper. (6–8 weeks)
- Phase 3 (GA): default streaming surface moves to AOF; legacy behavior available under opt-out flag for 2 months.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Storage retention for tx_token mapping vs cost. Default 7 days is a starting point; need finance input for storage budget.
- How to support long-running transactions where external systems do not expose idempotency (bank transfers). Potential options: mandate client-supplied idempotency keys or provide compensating workflow templates.
- UX for clients that only understand raw text streams (cURL, simple sockets). Need a backward-compatible human-friendly wire mode or a translator gateway.

Next steps / action items (owners):
- Engineering (Ravi) prototype AOF emitter + simple RTT store (2 sprints).
- SDK (Jordan) implement watchStream JS prototype and localStorage checkpoint helper (1 sprint).
- Product (Maya) recruit 3 pilot customers and draft integration checklist.
- Security (Sofia) review transaction token leakage and KMS requirements for storing token->result mappings.

Appendix: small client example (JS pseudo):
const s = watchStream({
  requestId: 'req-42',
  onFrame: frame => {
    if (frame.type === 'record') renderItem(frame.payload);
    if (frame.type === 'tool_commit') applyToolResult(frame.payload);
    if (frame.type === 'checkpoint') saveCheckpoint(frame.checkpoint_token);
  },
  resumeFrom: localStorage.getItem('last-cp')
});

Why this is different from prior designs:
- Rather than pushing more complex merging semantics to clients or forcing them to use final-output buffering, AOF shifts the boundary: the server guarantees atomicity at a frame level and the platform tracks transaction outcomes so clients can resume safely. The SDK provides opinionated, small helpers rather than a heavy-handed orchestration layer.

Risks:
- Implementation complexity in the runtime for framing and durable mapping.
- Potential increase in bandwidth (frame headers) and storage cost for transaction mapping.
- Customer adoption friction if existing integrations depend on raw text streaming behavior.

Concluding note:
This design aims to reduce developer cognitive load and operational accidents around partial streaming output and side-effectful tool calls. The goal is pragmatic: provide clear, small guarantees that unlock common patterns (incremental UX, safe tool integrations, mobile resume) without forcing every team to build bespoke dedup and checkpoint logic.
